title: The ascetics I have seen
hook: the poet has seen hosts of monks, siddhas and yogis, yet without love for the Lord it is all worth nothing (Savaiye 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tav prasad, and your line, by your grace. Did something good arrive today that you didn't plan for? Now the first of the ten verses. Day three hundred sixty-three.

Imagine a traveler who has made it his business to see every holy person in the land. He's sat outside the huts of ascetics who've given up everything. He's watched yogis hold impossible postures for hours. He's met celibates, wonder-workers, wandering monks, holy men of every order, in every region he could reach. Some of them were truly impressive. Some of them could do things you and I can't. At the end of all that traveling, he sits down to write what he's learned, and it comes out in one breath. Today: the ascetics I have seen.
screen: `A TRAVELER WHO HAS SEEN THEM ALL.` → `ASCETICS, YOGIS, MONKS.` → `WHAT DID HE LEARN?`

segments.voice: That traveler is the voice of the first savaiya. In paraphrase, it goes like this: I have wandered and seen hosts of pure ascetics, siddhas, the dwellings of yogis and celibates. I have seen heroes and gods and sages, and the holy men of sect after sect, the religious ways of every country. Then the last line turns, and it's the whole point: without the love and grace of the Lord, all of this isn't worth one ratti. A ratti is a tiny red seed, one of the smallest weights a jeweler used to weigh gold. So the verse puts the whole parade of holiness on a scale and it doesn't move the needle. Now, this is easy to hear wrong. It isn't sneering at discipline. These are people the poet respects enough to travel to see. The Sikh Gurus didn't ask their followers to leave home and live in a cave, but they didn't mock those who did. The savaiya's point is narrower and harder. You can do the most demanding spiritual thing there is, sit for years, give up food, give up sleep, and if love isn't at the center of it, it's weightless. And notice, the savaiya isn't only about other people's practices. Sikhs often hear it as a mirror. You can wear the right clothes, say the right banis, stand in the right places at the gurdwara, and miss the one thing that counts. That's why it's said in the morning. Before you do anything spiritual today, the verse asks what's at the center of it. The answer it gives is one word. Love.
screen: `HE HAS SEEN EVERY KIND OF HOLY ONE.` · `WITHOUT LOVE, NOT ONE RATTI.` · `NOT A SNEER AT DISCIPLINE.` · `A MIRROR FOR THE MORNING.` · then, large: `NOTHING WITHOUT LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing with love, not show. Settle in and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you'll do today that could be done either way. Making someone's coffee. Answering a hard message. Helping at home. Picture doing it the show way: wanting it noticed, keeping a little count. Then picture doing it the other way, for the person, with nothing in it for you. Notice how different the two feel, even in your imagination. If you pray, you can let Waheguru rest on your breath. Then choose the second way, and when the moment comes today, do it like that. The bell holds the time.
The ascetics I have seen. The first savaiya: a traveler sees every kind of holy discipline, and weighs it all without love at less than one ratti, a jeweler's tiny seed.
screen: `THE ASCETICS I HAVE SEEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nothing without love. Today, before one thing you do for someone, check what's at the center of it. If it's love, carry on. If it's show, start again quietly. Day three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as the first of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, and it is often explained in the gurdwara as a warning against outward religion without love.

fork.setup: you're the traveler. you have seen ascetics, yogis, monks and holy men of every order. you sit down to write what it all adds up to. what do you write?
options: without love, none of it is worth a single ratti.
fork.reveal: the savaiya weighs the whole parade of holiness and finds it weighs nothing without the love and grace of the Lord. it doesn't call anyone a fraud.

original.note: Gurmukhi: prem, love. the word these savaiye keep coming back to, and the thing the parade lacks.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem dismissing holy people.
what it means: a traveler weighs every kind of discipline and finds that without love it isn't worth one ratti.
what a scholar hears: the verse names shravaks, siddhas, yogis and celibates, the admired renouncers of the Guru's India, and the ratti, a seed used to weigh gold and gems, as its measure.

notes: Savaiya 1 paraphrased (the poet has seen shravaks, siddhas, yogis, jatis, heroes, gods, sages and holy men of many sects; without the love and grace of the Lord all are not worth one ratti). Confirm the paraphrase and the reading of 'ek ratee bin ek ratee ke'.
Ratti: the seed of Abrus precatorius, traditionally used as a small unit of weight for gold and gems. Confirm.

The verse names the shravak (associated with Jain ascetics) among others; the script deliberately does not single out any tradition and stresses that the verse does not sneer. Keeper to confirm this framing is fair.
Statement that the Gurus did not ask followers to renounce home life but did not mock those who did: confirm phrasing.
Reading the verse as a mirror for Sikhs' own practice: a common gurdwara reading; confirm.
